story.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers

facts.text: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.
They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers.
This story Ford Promises Not to Sell Drivers' Data After General Motors Privacy Scandal first appeared on First for Autos .

"We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit.

As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share.

While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news."
Ford says it will never sell your driving data to brokers or insurers, and its new website lets you adjust privacy settings anytime.
Turning off connected services can disable features such as BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle location services in the Ford app.
Real-time navigation and built-in roadside assistance may also stop working.
According to industry polling , only 14% of customers fully understand what their car collects.
Meanwhile, Ford surveyed over 1,000 consumers for this launch and found 91% believe data privacy is a key consideration when choosing a vehicle.
Ford says its connected vehicles collect three types of information: vehicle diagnostics, driving characteristics, and location data.
This data also helps Ford troubleshoot problems, improve future vehicles, and personalize your driving experience.
Your connected car knows more about your daily driving habits than you realize.
This is why Ford unveiled its new Privacy Promise to keep your vehicle data safe and let you control what you share.

If your Ford was built in 2018 or later, you can manage these settings right from your vehicle’s screen.
Ford’s privacy resources for Lincoln owners, and those residing in Mexico & Canada, are rolling out in the coming weeks, with more countries expected afterward.
General Motors agreed to pay $220 million across 36 states to resolve allegations that it shared driving and location data with data brokers and insurers without adequate consent.
Ford’s new “Privacy Promise” arrives in that context.
“We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones told TechCrunch.
